newsitem.title: FRANCE: French stocks close at new record high.
newsitem.headline: French stocks close at new record high.

text.p: French shares extended their gains in afternoon trade, boosted by Wall Street's early advance on supportive U.S. data, to set a fresh closing high on Tuesday.
The blue-chip CAC-40 index finished up 85.78 points or 3.0 percent at 2,944.04 while the CAC-40 futures contract ended 30 points higher at 2,948.0.
"It has been storming ahead," said one trader. "There has been quite a bit of activity on the Balladur bond. People are going into CAC-40 futures and a lot are going into the CAC-40."
Supporting the shares in recent sessions have been a firm dollar and a strong Wall Street.
But an extra lift has come from belief it will benefit from a mountain of cash the government is due to hand investors on July 16 when the "Balladur" bond expires.

The government is slated to return 91 billion francs to investors from a 1993 bond issued by former conservative prime minister Edouard Balladur to fund an economic recovery programme and a sizeable chunk is expected to go into the equity market.
"Traders will be worried about being short the market and being in a bear squeeze and that is what we may be in the grips of for the next couple of weeks," said one analyst.
Turnover totalled 11.30 billion francs, of which 8.5 billion was on CAC-40 stocks.
The previous closing record was set last Thursday.

Among the biggest movers were dollar plays, such as tyre-maker Michelin and beauty products firm L'Oreal, which traders said were in line to benefit from the franc's weakness against the U.S. currency.
Michelin closed up 7.14 percent at 378.10 francs, while L'Oreal finished 4.96 percent higher at 2,584.

Luxury goods firm LVMH rose 1.20 percent to 1,599 ahead of a meeting on Wednesday with Guinness and Grand Metropolitan. British newspapers say Guinness and Grand Met may propose to include Moet Hennessy, the drinks group controlled by LVMH, in their planned megamerger.

Channel tunnel operator Eurotunnel rose 6.98 percent to 6.90 francs on hopes of approval of its debt restructuring deal. After the market's close, the French government said Britain and France were ready to extend the group''s concession to at least 99 years, up from 65 years, under certain conditions.
